clue.text: Associate of mole, possibly Russian, as recorded by Leonov?

definitions.meaning: in The Wind in the Willows the stern woodland friend of Mole and Ratty is this animal

definitions.text: possibly Russian, as recorded by Leonov?
definitions.meaning: Leonid Leonov's first novel was The ..., about Russian peasants hiding in the forest

explanation.walkthrough: Two literary readings: Kenneth Grahame's riverbank animals, and the title of Leonid Leonov's 1924 Russian novel.
explanation.definitionFit: The burrowing animal is Mole's gruff friend in Grahame's book, and Leonov titled his novel after such animals.

parts.note: Jules Barbey d'Aurevilly wrote the novel Un ___ impossible, so the missing French word is a love affair

explanation.walkthrough: The clue completes a French title: Barbey d'Aurevilly's 1841 novel Un amour impossible.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for love or a love affair fills the gap in Barbey d'Aurevilly's novel title.

clue.text: New lodger, heavily disguised, is Hotspur's ally

indicators.note: a disguise changes appearance completely, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A new tenant in heavy disguise turns out to be a rebel from Shakespeare's Henry IV.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heavily disguised' rearranges NEW LODGER; in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1 the Welsh leader Owen Glendower rebels alongside Hotspur.
explanation.definitionFit: Owen Glendower, the Welsh rebel, joins Harry Hotspur's revolt against the king in Henry IV Part 1.

definitions.meaning: in crosswords a flower is something that flows, a stream
in Jane Eyre, St John, Diana and Mary, who take Jane in, prove to be her cousins

explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowers' reads as blooms but means things that flow; the second sense is the family surname in Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre.
explanation.definitionFit: Streams are things that flow, and the Rivers siblings in Brontë's novel turn out to be Jane's cousins.

clue.text: More daughter in broken cart on island

indicators.note: something broken is in pieces, so the letters of the word cart are rearranged

parts.note: Iona is a small island of the Inner Hebrides off Scotland

explanation.surface: Somebody's daughter is found in a broken-down cart on a Scottish island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges CART to CATR. The definition is the heroine of Stevenson's sequel to Kidnapped, daughter of James More Drummond.
explanation.definitionFit: In Stevenson's novel the title heroine is the child of the Highland rogue James More.

clue.text: Gibbons' decline and fall of rural England?

definitions.text: Gibbons' decline and fall of rural England?

parts.words: Gibbons' decline and fall of rural England?
parts.note: Stella Gibbons's comic novel of a decaying Sussex farm, punning on Edward Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire

explanation.walkthrough: The clue swaps the historian Gibbon for the novelist Stella Gibbons, whose 1932 parody of rustic novels shows a farm in decay.
explanation.definitionFit: Stella Gibbons's 1932 novel parodies gloomy rustic fiction about a crumbling farming family.

clue.text: Sosekinovel perceived by McCullers as solitary pursuer

definitions.meaning: Natsume Soseki's novel Kokoro is known in English under this title

definitions.text: perceived by McCullers as solitary pursuer
definitions.meaning: Carson McCullers's novel calls this organ a lonely hunter

explanation.walkthrough: The page runs 'Soseki novel' together. Kokoro is translated with this title, and McCullers's title is The Heart Is a Lonely Hunter.
explanation.definitionFit: Soseki's Kokoro is rendered in English with this title, and McCullers's novel names this organ a lonely hunter.

clue.text: "Humility is a duty in great ones, as well as in —s" (Jeremy Taylor)

definitions.text: "Humility is a duty in great ones, as well as in —s" (Jeremy Taylor)

parts.words: "Humility is a duty in great ones, as well as in —s" (Jeremy Taylor)
parts.note: the missing word in the quotation from the divine Jeremy Taylor is the opposite of great ones, a fool

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from the seventeenth-century bishop Jeremy Taylor; Dostoevsky's novel title fits too.
explanation.definitionFit: Taylor contrasts the great with simpletons, fools of no standing.

clue.text: At the end of the day, Asimov produced it

definitions.meaning: the close of the day when darkness comes
Isaac Asimov's celebrated 1941 short story, later a novel, has this title

explanation.walkthrough: 'At the end of the day' sounds like a stock phrase, but it holds the literal sense of dusk; Asimov wrote the famous story of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Dusk is when darkness falls at day's end, and Asimov titled his story about a world seeing stars for the first time so.

definitions.meaning: an Oxford college, founded for women in 1879
Edith ... co-wrote the Irish R.M. stories with Martin Ross

explanation.walkthrough: An Oxford college and the Irish novelist Edith Somerville share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxford college bears the same name as Edith Somerville, the Irish author of Some Experiences of an Irish R.M.

clue.text: Like a villain, I leave article in the middle

explanation.surface: A self-confessed villain slips away leaving an article behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the middle' puts A inside GO, after I. The villain is the schemer of Shakespeare's Othello.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Iago is a byword for a scheming villain in Othello.

clue.text: Name given to the Carnival's 'creator (after Chopin rather than Delius)

definitions.text: Name given to the Carnival's 'creator (after Chopin rather than Delius)

parts.words: Name given to the Carnival's 'creator (after Chopin rather than Delius)
parts.note: the creator's first name, spelt the way the Polish composer spelt it, without the final letter Delius used

explanation.walkthrough: Chopin's first name was spelt without a final K, while Delius's had one; the clue asks for the shorter spelling.
explanation.definitionFit: The forename is spelt as Chopin's was, not with the K of Delius's.

definitions.meaning: Isaac Bashevis Singer wrote the novel The ..., sequel to The Manor
landed holdings or possessions

explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' is not a vocalist but the Yiddish novelist Isaac Bashevis Singer.
explanation.definitionFit: Singer's novel bears this title, and the word also means land or possessions owned.

parts.note: SP is the starting price in horse-race betting
E and W are the compass directions east and west

explanation.surface: Someone is thrown out over a betting system and given directions.
explanation.walkthrough: SP, the starting price, is the odds at which British racecourse bets are settled.
explanation.definitionFit: To vomit or spout something is to eject it forcibly.

clue.text: Spoil a lie about composer of I Barbiere di Seviglia

definitions.text: composer of I Barbiere di Seviglia

indicators.note: about here means turned around and jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is told to stop spoiling an opera with a lie about its composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges SPOIL A LIE. Giovanni Paisiello wrote a Barber of Seville decades before Rossini.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Paisiello's 1782 opera on Beaumarchais's comedy preceded Rossini's version.

definitions.meaning: the Comte de ... was a leader of the early French Revolution
a Paris Metro station is named after him

explanation.walkthrough: A French revolutionary statesman and a stop on the Paris Metro share the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Honoré Gabriel Riqueti, Comte de Mirabeau, led the 1789 revolution, and a Paris Metro stop bears his name.

parts.note: Fiammetta, Italian for little flame, was the muse of the author of the Decameron

explanation.walkthrough: Fiammetta means 'little flame' in Italian; she is the beloved of the Decameron's author.
explanation.definitionFit: The Decameron author celebrated his muse Fiammetta in several works.

indicators.note: doing something playfully means in a jumbled fashion, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone gives a fitting playwright a teasing nudge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playfully' rearranges PRODS APT. Tom Stoppard wrote Arcadia and Rosencrantz and Guildenstern Are Dead.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Stoppard is a celebrated British dramatist.

parts.note: the Italian term literally means a small book, and it holds the words of an opera

explanation.walkthrough: The Italian term is literally a diminutive of the word for book, and it is the text of an opera.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian word means a small book and names the text sung in an opera.

definitions.meaning: Old King ... is the merry old soul of the nursery rhyme
G. D. H. ... was a writer on political economy and socialism

explanation.walkthrough: Old King Cole is the nursery rhyme; G. D. H. Cole was the Oxford socialist economist.
explanation.definitionFit: The nursery-rhyme monarch and the Oxford economist G. D. H. Cole share the name.

definitions.meaning: to join metal pieces by fusing them on, two words
fey sounds like Fay

explanation.walkthrough: 'reportedly fey' is the sound of the forename Fay: the novelist is Fay Weldon.
explanation.definitionFit: Fusing metal parts together fixes them firmly, and Fay Weldon wrote The Life and Loves of a She-Devil.

parts.note: kirk is the Scottish word for church

explanation.surface: A church is lifted up to honour a disputed figure from the north-east.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet James Kirkup, from the north-east of England, provoked a blasphemy trial in 1977.
explanation.definitionFit: The poet James Kirkup, born near the River Wear, caused the 1977 blasphemy prosecution of Gay News.

clue.text: Invoke blessing to reveal Oxford intellectual

indicators.note: the letters appear across the two words, revealing themselves inside the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone invokes a blessing to reveal a great Oxford mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to reveal' shows KEBLE inside invoKE BLEssing. John Keble led the Oxford Movement, and Keble College is named for him.
explanation.definitionFit: John Keble, the poet and churchman, led the Oxford Movement.

definitions.meaning: Virginia Woolf's 1931 novel
in the patriotic song Rule, Britannia! Britannia rules these

explanation.walkthrough: Virginia Woolf's experimental novel shares its title with what 'Rule, Britannia!' says Britannia rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's 1931 novel has this title, and the anthem says Britannia rules the sea's breakers.

clue.text: Stopover by Bourget (to change planes perhaps?)

definitions.meaning: a French word for a stage or halt on a journey
Paul Bourget wrote the 1902 novel L'Etape

explanation.walkthrough: The French word for a halt between stages is also the title of a Paul Bourget novel; the parenthesis plays on Le Bourget airport.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a halt on a journey is the title of Bourget's novel.

clue.text: Chesterton booked one of strange occupations

definitions.text: Chesterton booked one of strange occupations

parts.words: Chesterton booked one of strange occupations
parts.note: G. K. Chesterton's book The ___ of Queer Trades, strange occupations being queer trades

explanation.walkthrough: Chesterton's 1905 collection is The Club of Queer Trades: 'strange occupations' restates 'queer trades'.
explanation.definitionFit: Chesterton's stories tell of a society whose members follow queer trades.

definitions.meaning: the church of Laodicea in Revelation was neither hot nor cold, so its name means half-hearted
Thomas Hardy's 1881 novel is titled after such a half-hearted person

explanation.walkthrough: In Revelation the church at Laodicea is rebuked for being neither hot nor cold; Hardy used the term as a novel title.
explanation.definitionFit: A person half-hearted in belief, like the Laodicean church of Revelation, gives Hardy's 1881 novel its title.

clue.text: Old venom possibly found in the world of fiction

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters could form something else, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Old venom might be found among novelists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' rearranges OLD VENOM.
explanation.definitionFit: The realm of novels and novelists is the world of fiction.

parts.note: the gap in Dorothy Parker's poem Resume is filled by hangman's loops of rope

explanation.walkthrough: Dorothy Parker's poem 'Résumé' lists ways to die: 'Guns aren't lawful; / Nooses give'.
explanation.definitionFit: Parker's poem lists hangman's ropes among unsatisfactory ways to die.
